title: Spent this year fixing "AI-built" games for indie devs. Same handful of issues every time
author: makeitschooly
selftext:
I do contract work for solo devs who vibe coded their game with Cursor or Claude or whatever and now need help before/after launch. Pattern is always the same. Game works fine in their own playtesting, they're proud of it, honestly fair, it runs. Then real players get their hands on it and things break in ways the dev never saw coming because they were the only person who ever touched the thing.

Stuff I run into basically every project:

1. API keys or backend secrets just sitting in the client build. If your game hits a leaderboard, save server, anything, go check your build for stuff a player could pull out of your APK in five minutes.

2. The client trusts itself. Score, currency, inventory, whatever gets sent up and the server just accepts it, no check. Someone edits a save file or messes with a request and now they've got infinite gems. It's not if, it's when.

3. No separation between player accounts. Cloud saves or multiplayer and player A can read or overwrite player B's stuff just by changing an ID somewhere. Nobody catches this in solo testing because there's only ever one of you.

4. Nothing tracks crashes once it's out in the wild. Players don't email you a bug report, they just uninstall and leave a 1 star review that just says "broken." Slapping in basic crash logging takes like 20 minutes and tells you exactly where people are quitting.

5. Backups that have never actually been tested. Everyone says they have them. Almost nobody has restored one. Until you do that once you don't really know.

6. IAP trusting the client on price or purchase state. First person with a proxy tool will wreck your economy in a day.

The AI specific one: it'll quietly touch systems you weren't even asking about while it's fixing something else. Your movement code was fine last night, you didn't go near it, now it's acting weird. Keep one test scene you click through after any big AI assisted change, catches this fast.

None of it is a rewrite, it's a couple days of boring work. Way better to eat that before launch than after your Discord blows up.

Curious what everyone else keeps running into that's not on here.

replies.author: RedTheRobot
replies.body:
So before I actually got a job in programming I was super scare I wouldn't be good enough. So I worked retail for 12 years because it was safe, for me. Then new management came in and that fun, safe environment was no longer that. I even had the first and only panic attack of my life. So I started looking and saw a great opportunity. The interview was even more crazy as I had the head of HR say to the CEO I don't know why we are hiring for this position when the technology is going away. They offered me the job but at $17 which was a $5 pay cut. I said I could do that so they said they could do $18 after the 1 month trial. So I agreed and left retail.

Now to get to the point of the story. All my worry of not being good enough. All my concern of would I be able to do the job was for nothing. The code that I looked at was not the best written at the time and I even improved things that saved the company money. My strongest memory was when I had a PM ask if I could sit next to another programmer who was newly hired but was older than me and had more professional experience than me but I had to sit there and help him fix his code because he broke the test environment. Did I forget to mention the company had no source control. That is where it really hit me, that I am not as green as I think I am.

comments.author: sevenoutdb
comments.body:
Great list here. These are definitely issues I’ve seen time and time again from small teams that have never shipped a game before. There is a value to thinking big. 

One of the things I always tell teams is that there are no edge cases at 100k users, and how many angry customers can you deal with every day before your review scores are so deep down in a hole that you can’t dig out. No one will download free game with terrible review scores and absolutely no one will buy a discounted game with a shitty review score.

comments.author: Vivid_Gas_5755
comments.body: The AI touching systems you did not ask it to is the one that bit us hardest. We were using a few different tools to prototype a persistent world sim (been testing worldos for that kind of thing on the TTRPG side), and mid-session the model rewrote our event queue handling while it was supposed to be fixing a dialogue bug. Nothing broke immediately, which is actually the worst outcome because we shipped it. Found it two weeks later when world state started desynchronizing in ways that made no sense. We now have a smoke test that hits every major system after anything AI-assisted, which would have been obvious from the start if any of us had stopped celebrating that the dialogue bug was fixed.

comments.author: FitWorldliness5993
comments.body:
Extra stuff I would add

1) tell AI to do playtest sessions of the game if you don't have time to do them  
2) tell the AI to do a security scrutiny if you have a multiplayer game  
3) tell AI to do bughunting session  
4) tell AI to do code refactor following clean code standards, tell it to construct the game modularly and follwoing single responsability wherever possible  
5) tell it to help you do a release plan and schedule

6) tell it to add automated tests to all important features preferably using known tests harness, most dev environments support some test harness aproach

7) tell it to help you setup a proper repo and CI/CD

comments.author: Dazzling-Extent-5137
comments.body:
I will argue this - there's a big difference between someone without a programming background using AI to build something and someone with a programming background using AI to build something.

The more you've worked in the field the more you know what to tell AI to cover or check, set boundaries, set up comprehensive testing and so on.

Otherwise, I will note what a lot of people already said - AI really isn't doing a lot of mistakes that low experience or not so great developers do in real life. They just usually have multiple sets of checks and balances, whether it's procedures, peer or tech lead code reviews, CI/CD automated checks, etc.
